domains.name: Phraseology & Formulaic Language
domains.summary: Phraseology & Formulaic Language treats multi-word units — collocations, lexical bundles, spoken formulas and fixed expressions — as core carriers of academic meaning rather than decorative extras. Corpus research shows that expert academic writing and speech rely heavily on recurrent combinations whose functions differ (research-, text- and stance-oriented) and vary by discipline, and that L2 and novice writers tend to underuse, misuse or overuse them. The domain also develops strategies (corpus consultation, critical use of phrase resources) so that learners can verify phraseology independently, while guarding against formulaic, template-driven text.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to notice and use the word combinations that academic writers and lecturers rely on, and to check combinations yourself with corpora and phrase resources without filling your writing with stock phrases.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build the habit of noticing and recording combinations, with frequent academic collocations and text-organising bundles from course materials.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Extend collocational range, introduce research- and stance-oriented bundles linked to calibration, and train learners in collocation dictionaries, simple corpus searches and critical phrasebank use.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work on learners' own drafts: repair persistent miscollocations, reduce overused connectors and stance frames, and compare bundles with those in disciplinary texts.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Prioritise discipline-relevant collocations and bundles for source-based writing, checked against field texts in a compressed timeframe.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Profile the phraseology of target journals with self-built corpora and refine stance formulas for research writing and publication.

domains.name: Register & Academic Style
domains.summary: Register & Academic Style develops learners' ability to read a communicative situation and choose language accordingly: register as a configuration of field, tenor and mode; the systematic differences in how speech and writing package meaning; and the features conventionally associated with formal academic prose. The domain deliberately treats style 'rules' as probabilistic tendencies to be tested against evidence of disciplinary and historical variation, frames impersonality as a choice about agency rather than a route to objectivity, and extends to inclusive language and to writing for non-specialist readers.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why academic writing and speech sound the way they do, how to adjust your style for different readers, purposes and disciplines, and how to tell real conventions from over-simplified 'rules'.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build register awareness through concrete contrasts (email, forum post, assignment) and an explicit, reasoned checklist of formality features, including precise rather than vague reference.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Make spoken–written differences and formality choices explicit tools for reading-into-writing and presentations, and begin testing prescriptive style rules against exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Reconcile conflicting module advice by examining disciplinary style, authorial presence and density in the student's own field and genres.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Calibrate density, impersonality and inclusive description for compressed source-based and professional writing, often in an unfamiliar discipline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Align style with target journals and examiners' fields, claim contribution with appropriate presence, and write lay summaries and engagement texts for non-specialists.

domains.name: Academic Vocabulary
domains.summary: Academic Vocabulary covers the lexical platform for university study: the vocabulary size and text coverage needed to read and listen independently; the general academic, sub-technical and technical layers of university lexis; the word-level knowledge (morphology, word grammar, countability, spelling) needed for accurate production; and the strategies learners use to keep expanding vocabulary beyond the classroom. Academic word lists (AWL, AVL) are treated as useful but contested starting points, because the 'academic' status, meaning and frequency of items vary by discipline, and coverage thresholds are treated as approximate planning guides rather than cut-offs.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn which words are most worth your time for university study, how to learn and remember them efficiently, and how to use them accurately and precisely in your own writing and speaking.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Secure the high-frequency base, word families and the vocabulary of university study and assignments, and establish independent learning routines with dictionaries and word cards.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Build general academic vocabulary with its word grammar and collocations, set realistic size goals from coverage research, and practise inferring and checking meaning from context.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Move academic and sub-technical vocabulary into accurate productive use within the student's discipline, including process verbs, evaluative lexis and discipline-specific senses.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Prioritise disciplinary terminology, lexical precision and evaluation for source-based writing on compressed one-year programmes.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine precision, shell nouns and evaluative lexis for research writing, using evidence from the target field's literature.

topics.name: Collocation awareness
topics.description: Understand that words habitually co-occur with particular other words (collocation) and that many meanings are carried by multi-word units rather than single words, and notice such units when reading and listening. This awareness is the basis for learning vocabulary in chunks, for natural-sounding production and for using collocation resources.
masteryEvidence: Identifies collocations and other multi-word units in an academic text and records them as units
Explains why a grammatically possible combination (e.g. 'make research') sounds wrong to expert readers
Distinguishes free combinations, restricted collocations and fixed expressions with examples
Records new vocabulary with typical collocates and an example rather than as an isolated word
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 100-word academic paragraph and ask the learner to underline the word combinations most worth learning as units. Check whether they select verb–noun, adjective–noun and preposition-based combinations (e.g. 'play a role', 'a significant increase', 'in terms of') rather than isolated difficult words.

topics.name: Academic collocations
topics.description: Recognise and use frequent academic collocations — verb–noun ('conduct research', 'draw a conclusion', 'raise a question'), adjective–noun ('a significant difference', 'empirical evidence') and noun–preposition combinations ('an increase in', 'the effect on') — so that writing and speech express academic meanings in conventional, readily processed forms.
masteryEvidence: Uses a range of verb–noun and adjective–noun academic collocations accurately in writing
Selects collocates that fit the intended meaning (e.g. 'raise' versus 'address' a question)
Draws collocations from an academic collocation list or corpus and records them with examples
Uses strongly associated, less frequent collocations as well as very frequent general ones
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give ten academic nouns from a recent reading (e.g. evidence, hypothesis, impact, conclusion, gap) and ask for a sentence using each with an appropriate verb and adjective. Check accuracy and range: look beyond 'big impact' and 'make a conclusion' for combinations such as 'a substantial impact' and 'reach a conclusion'.

topics.name: Verb–noun collocation accuracy
topics.description: Avoid and repair verb–noun miscollocations that arise when learners transfer combinations from another language or overextend general delexical verbs (e.g. 'make research', 'do a mistake', 'rise a question'), by identifying their own recurrent errors and checking combinations with collocation dictionaries or corpora. Verb–noun errors are among the most persistent lexical errors even in advanced learner writing.
masteryEvidence: Identifies verb–noun miscollocations in own and others' writing
Repairs miscollocations using a collocation dictionary or corpus and records the conventional verb
Chooses accurately between delexical verbs (make, do, have, take, give) with common academic nouns
Distinguishes transitive and intransitive verb pairs that affect collocation (raise/rise)
Maintains a personal list of recurrent errors and checks drafts against it before submission
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph containing five verb–noun errors (e.g. 'make an experiment', 'rise the issue', 'do progress', 'make a research', 'give attention on') and five acceptable combinations, including one that varies between varieties ('take/make a decision'). Ask the learner to correct the errors without changing the acceptable items and to say how they checked.

topics.name: Research-oriented lexical bundles
topics.description: Recognise and use research-oriented lexical bundles — recurrent word sequences that structure content about the research world, such as location, procedure, quantification and description ('the extent to which', 'in the case of', 'the nature of the', 'at the same time', 'on the basis of') — together with their typical grammatical continuations. These bundles are frequent in expert writing, vary by discipline and help writers express relations between concepts economically.
masteryEvidence: Recognises common research-oriented bundles and identifies their function in context (e.g. quantification, description, procedure)
Completes bundles grammatically with an appropriate continuation (e.g. 'the extent to which' + clause)
Uses several research-oriented bundles accurately in own writing
Identifies which bundles are frequent in texts from their own discipline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five bundles ('the extent to which', 'in the case of', 'the nature of the', 'on the basis of', 'the relationship between') and ask for one sentence with each about the learner's field. Check grammatical completion (e.g. 'the extent to which X affects Y', not 'the extent to which of X') and that each bundle performs a sensible function.

topics.name: Text-oriented lexical bundles
topics.description: Use text-oriented bundles that organise discourse and signal relations between ideas — transition ('on the other hand', 'in addition to the'), result ('as a result of'), structuring ('in the next section') and framing ('in terms of the', 'with respect to the') — with accurate meaning and grammar and without overuse. These bundles support cohesion and help readers navigate a text.
masteryEvidence: Uses common text-oriented bundles with accurate meaning and grammar
Distinguishes bundles that signal contrast, addition, result, framing and structure
Uses 'on the other hand' only to introduce a contrasting alternative, not any additional point
Avoids beginning most sentences with a transition bundle
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph in which 'on the other hand' and 'in addition' begin almost every sentence, some with the wrong meaning. Ask for a revision. Check that the learner corrects meaning errors (e.g. 'on the other hand' used for addition), reduces overuse and uses other cohesive means where appropriate.

topics.name: Stance and engagement bundles
topics.description: Use stance and engagement bundles — largely impersonal frames expressing likelihood, importance, necessity or evidentiality ('it is possible that', 'it is important to', 'it should be noted that', 'as can be seen') — to position claims and guide readers, matching the frame's strength to the evidence and avoiding formulaic overuse.
masteryEvidence: Uses anticipatory-it stance bundles accurately with the right complement (that-clause or to-infinitive)
Distinguishes bundles that express likelihood, importance, necessity and evidence
Selects a frame whose strength matches the evidence for the claim
Avoids stacking several stance frames in one sentence or relying on one frame repeatedly
Recognises reader-directed bundles ('as can be seen', 'it should be noted that') and their guiding function
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three claims with different evidence bases (one small study, a meta-analysis, the writer's own interpretation) and ask the learner to introduce each with a suitable stance frame. Check calibration (e.g. 'it is possible that' versus 'there is strong evidence that'), grammatical completion and variety.

topics.name: Spoken academic formulas
topics.description: Recognise and use formulas typical of lectures, seminars and presentations ('what I want to do is', 'if you look at', 'the point is', 'I'd like to come back to') that organise talk, focus attention and manage interaction. Recognising them supports lecture comprehension; producing them supports fluent, well-structured speaking.
masteryEvidence: Identifies formulas that signal topic shifts, emphasis, examples and returns to the main point in authentic lectures
Uses spoken formulas to structure a short presentation or seminar contribution
Distinguishes spoken formulas from their written equivalents and avoids carrying spoken forms into essays
Produces formulas fluently as single units, including in reduced forms
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a three-minute lecture extract and ask the learner to note each phrase that signals what is coming or what matters, and what it signals. Then ask for a one-minute unscripted explanation of a concept using three such formulas. Check recognition accuracy and natural, fluent use.

topics.name: Fixed expressions, idioms and binomials
topics.description: Recognise idioms, binomials and other relatively fixed expressions ('pros and cons', 'by and large', 'trial and error', 'to a greater or lesser extent', 'in the long run') in academic texts and lectures and judge their register, using them in writing only where they are conventional and avoiding conversational idioms in formal prose.
masteryEvidence: Interprets common fixed expressions and idioms met in lectures and readings
Classifies fixed expressions as acceptable in formal writing, typical of speech, or genre-dependent
Reproduces fixed expressions in their conventional form and order (e.g. 'pros and cons')
Replaces conversational idioms in drafts with register-appropriate alternatives
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give ten expressions (e.g. 'by and large', 'a piece of cake', 'trial and error', 'at the end of the day', 'to a lesser extent'). Ask the learner to sort them into 'suitable for an essay', 'speech only' and 'depends on genre', and justify two choices. Check register judgement and conventional form.

topics.name: Consulting corpora for usage
topics.description: Use concordancers and academic corpora, including small self-built corpora, to check collocation, frequency, grammatical patterns and register while writing — a data-driven learning approach that lets learners answer their own usage questions and interpret the evidence critically.
masteryEvidence: Turns a usage doubt (e.g. which preposition follows 'impact') into a corpus query
Runs word, phrase and wildcard searches in an available academic corpus tool and sorts concordance lines
Identifies the most frequent pattern and acceptable variants from concordance evidence
Compares sub-corpora or filters to check register or discipline
Explains the limits of a search result (corpus size and composition, low frequencies)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to decide between 'impact on', 'impact to' and 'impact for' using a corpus tool, showing the query and the evidence. Check whether the search is efficient, frequencies are interpreted sensibly and genuine variation is noted.

topics.name: Using phrasebanks critically
topics.description: Use function-organised phrase resources (academic phrasebanks, formula lists) to find conventional language for rhetorical moves — introducing a topic, reporting findings, acknowledging limitations — while adapting phrases to one's own content and avoiding formulaic, template-driven text in which phrases substitute for ideas.
masteryEvidence: Locates phrases for a target rhetorical function in a phrase resource
Adapts a phrase grammatically and semantically to own content
Chooses among options according to strength, register and discipline
Revises drafts that over-rely on stock phrases so that content carries the argument
Distinguishes reusing generic academic phrasing from reusing source-specific wording
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write the limitations paragraph of a short report with a phrasebank open, then explain how they adapted two phrases. Check that phrases fit the content and grammar, are not stacked, and that the learner can explain why generic phrasing is acceptable while copying a source's distinctive wording is not.

topics.name: Register and situational variation
topics.description: Recognise that language varies systematically with the situation of use — the activity and subject matter (field), the relationship between participants (tenor) and the channel and role of language (mode) — and that formality is a continuum rather than a binary. This lets learners explain why a seminar contribution, a lab report and an email to a tutor are worded differently, and adjust their own language accordingly.
masteryEvidence: Describes a text's situation of use in terms of subject matter, participants' relationship and channel, and links at least two linguistic features to those factors
Places several texts on the same topic (e.g. lecture transcript, textbook paragraph, forum post, student email) on a formality continuum and justifies the order with linguistic evidence
Rewrites a short message for a different reader or channel, changing grammar and organisation as well as individual words
Explains why a feature that is normal in one academic register (e.g. 'you' in a lecture) is marked in another (e.g. a research report)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three short texts on one topic (lecture extract, textbook paragraph, email to a tutor). Ask the learner who is communicating with whom, through what channel, and to point to three features in each that reflect this. Look for features tied to situational factors (pronouns and greetings to tenor; contractions and repetition to mode), not impressionistic labels such as 'uses more academic words'.

topics.name: Spoken versus written academic language
topics.description: Understand how academic writing and academic speech package meaning differently: writing tends towards high lexical density and compressed noun phrases, whereas speech distributes meaning across chains of clauses, with repetition, discourse markers and direct address. Learners use this to unpack dense prose, follow lectures, and avoid carrying conversational clause-chaining into essays or essay-style density into presentations.
masteryEvidence: Rewrites a short spoken explanation as one or two written sentences that package the same content in fewer clauses and denser noun phrases
Unpacks a dense written sentence into a sequence of spoken-style clauses without losing the logical relations
Identifies features typical of academic speech in a lecture transcript (repetition, discourse markers, clause chaining, direct address) and explains how they help listeners
Explains why a presentation read from an essay script is hard for an audience to follow
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 40–60-word lecture transcript extract and ask the learner to write it as one or two textbook sentences; then give a dense written sentence and ask them to explain it aloud as a lecturer might. Check that processes become nouns and fillers disappear in the first task, and that agents, verbs and connectors are restored in the second, with content intact in both.

topics.name: Features of formal academic style
topics.description: Control the features conventionally associated with formal academic writing — avoiding contractions, colloquial vocabulary and conversational intensifiers, using direct questions and second-person address sparingly, and choosing pronouns deliberately — while understanding these as probabilistic tendencies that vary by genre and discipline rather than absolute rules. Control of these features lets writers meet reader expectations without adopting a stilted, over-formal voice.
masteryEvidence: Revises a paragraph to remove contractions, colloquialisms and conversational intensifiers (e.g. 'really', 'so', 'a lot of') using suitable alternatives
Recasts a sequence of rhetorical questions as statements or indirect questions where the genre calls for it
Distinguishes features that are almost always avoided in assessed prose (contractions) from those whose acceptability depends on genre and discipline (first person, sentence-initial 'But')
Avoids over-correction, such as replacing everyday words with rare Latinate synonyms
Justifies stylistic choices in a draft by reference to genre and reader
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an 80-word informal paragraph (contractions, 'a lot of', 'you can see', a rhetorical question, 'really important') and ask for a revision for a coursework essay. Check that informal features are changed without over-formalisation ('a plethora of'), and ask the learner which changes were near-obligatory and which were judgement calls.

topics.name: Myths and change in academic style
topics.description: Evaluate prescriptive style 'rules' — never use I, never start a sentence with And or But, never split an infinitive, always prefer the passive — against evidence of what expert writers in a field actually do and how practice is changing. This replaces rule-following with informed choice and helps learners read assignment and journal guidance in the light of disciplinary norms.
masteryEvidence: Identifies a style rule as prescriptive and states what evidence would be needed to test it
Checks a style rule against a small sample of published texts in their field and reports the result
Distinguishes binding local requirements (module handbook, journal style sheet) from general conventions and from myths
Explains, with examples, how practice for one contested feature differs between two disciplines
Uses a contested feature deliberately and justifies the choice to a tutor or supervisor
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present the advice 'Never use I in academic writing' and ask the learner to evaluate it. A strong answer qualifies the rule by discipline, genre and function (e.g. 'I' for procedural decisions versus unsupported personal opinion), refers to evidence and notes that local guidance must still be checked; a weak answer accepts or rejects the rule absolutely.

topics.name: Impersonality and authorial presence
topics.description: Choose between impersonal constructions (agentless passive, anticipatory 'it', inanimate subjects such as 'this study') and visible authorial presence (first-person pronouns, explicit evaluation) according to discipline, genre and rhetorical purpose. Understanding that impersonal forms background agency rather than make claims objective lets writers decide where to foreground their own role, for example in methodological decisions or claims of contribution.
masteryEvidence: Identifies who is responsible for actions and claims in sentences built with passives, anticipatory 'it' and inanimate subjects
Rewrites an impersonal sentence with authorial presence, and vice versa, and explains what changes in focus and responsibility
Uses first person for procedural decisions or contribution claims where the discipline permits, and impersonal forms where agency is irrelevant or conventional
Explains why the passive does not make a claim more objective
Avoids ambiguous agency, such as dangling modifiers created by unnecessary passives
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a methods paragraph written entirely in agentless passives, including one researcher decision ('It was decided to exclude…'). Ask the learner to revise it for a discipline that accepts 'we'. Check that only decisions the writers are accountable for become agentive, that routine procedures stay passive, and that the learner can justify each choice.

topics.name: Information density and readability
topics.description: Balance the compressed phrasing typical of academic writing — nominalisation, long noun phrases, noun + noun sequences — against the intended reader's need to process the text, unpacking where density hides agency, causality or reference. Writers who control density can condense content for expert readers and loosen it for novices or mixed audiences.
masteryEvidence: Compresses a clause-heavy paragraph into fewer, denser sentences using nominalisation and noun-phrase modification without losing logical relations
Identifies sentences in own or others' writing where noun stacks or chained nominalisations obscure agents, causes or reference
Unpacks over-dense sentences by restoring verbs, agents or explicit relational words where the reader needs them
Adjusts density for a stated reader (e.g. specialist examiner versus first-year audience)
Explains the trade-off between concision and readability with reference to a specific sentence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a sentence such as 'Student retention rate improvement strategy evaluation outcomes were mixed.' Ask the learner to diagnose the problem and produce one version for a non-specialist and one for an expert report. Look for unpacking of the noun stack, restored relations (who improved what, how it was evaluated) and a defensible difference in density between versions.

topics.name: Avoiding vague and overgeneralised language
topics.description: Replace vague nouns and quantifiers ('things', 'stuff', 'a lot of', 'many aspects'), unbounded time references ('nowadays', 'since the dawn of time') and sweeping claims ('everyone knows', 'always', 'in all countries') with precise reference and bounded claims that could be supported. Vagueness and overgeneralisation weaken credibility because readers cannot tell exactly what is claimed or check it against evidence.
masteryEvidence: Identifies vague nouns, empty quantifiers and sweeping generalisations in a draft
Replaces vague nouns with specific nouns that name the referent (e.g. 'costs', 'policies', 'risk factors')
Replaces unbounded time and scope references with specific periods, places or populations
Converts a sweeping generalisation into a bounded claim using quantifiers, scope limitation or reference to evidence
Opens an essay with a specific context rather than a universal statement
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an essay opening such as 'Nowadays, technology is a very important thing in everyone's life and has a lot of effects.' and ask for a revision for an assignment on online learning in UK universities. Check for specific nouns, a bounded time, place and population, a claim that a source could support, and no new overstatement.

topics.name: Inclusive and bias-free language
topics.description: Refer to people accurately and respectfully: use gender-neutral wording (including singular 'they'), specific and current terms for groups, and person-first or identity-first language according to the conventions of the field and the preferences of the communities concerned. Inclusive language is now expected by most style guides, journals and ethics processes, and it usually improves precision as well as respect.
masteryEvidence: Revises generic masculine forms using plurals, singular 'they' or restructuring, consistently across a text
Describes groups at an appropriate level of specificity (e.g. age ranges, named conditions) rather than with broad or outdated labels
Locates and applies the bias-free language guidance of the required style guide or journal
Explains that person-first and identity-first language are both in use and that the choice depends on field and community preference
Omits characteristics such as gender, ethnicity or disability where they are irrelevant, and reports them precisely where they are analytically relevant
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a methods paragraph containing 'mankind', 'each participant… he', 'the elderly' and a disability label used as a noun. Ask for a revision following APA guidance. Check for consistent gender-neutral reference, more specific age description, an informed and justified choice between person-first and identity-first wording, and no loss of precision.

topics.name: Writing and speaking for non-specialist audiences
topics.description: Adapt specialist content for readers or listeners outside the field — lay summaries, participant information, public talks, blog posts — by selecting what matters to that audience, replacing or glossing technical terms, reducing density, using concrete examples, and keeping the expression of certainty faithful to the evidence. Students and researchers are increasingly required to communicate this way for ethics, funding, impact and engagement.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the technical terms, assumed knowledge and dense phrasing in a specialist text that a lay reader would not follow
Produces a lay summary that preserves the core finding and its main limitation in everyday language
Glosses unavoidable technical terms in context rather than deleting them
Uses concrete examples, analogies or statements of relevance suited to the audience
Retains appropriate expressions of uncertainty instead of overstating findings for impact
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 150-word research abstract from their field and ask for a 100-word lay summary for a university news page. Check that the main finding is accurate, jargon is removed or glossed, sentences are less dense, relevance is made explicit, and hedged findings have not become certainties or 'breakthroughs'.

topics.name: Disciplinary variation in style
topics.description: Understand how disciplines differ in style — frequency of first person, passive voice, hedging and boosting, citation forms and the way arguments are built — and relate these differences to how fields create and validate knowledge (e.g. hard/soft and pure/applied tendencies). This lets learners interpret conflicting advice from different modules and align their writing with their target discipline.
masteryEvidence: Describes two or three stylistic features of writing in their own discipline, with examples from published texts
Compares one feature (e.g. self-mention, hedging or integral citation) across two disciplines and relates the difference to knowledge-making practices
Explains conflicting style advice from different modules in terms of disciplinary or genre conventions
Adapts the style of a paragraph for a reader from a different discipline
Uses small-scale exemplar or corpus analysis to identify conventions in an unfamiliar field
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two short extracts on related topics, one from a hard-science journal and one from a social-science or humanities journal. Ask the learner to identify three stylistic differences and suggest why each arises. Look for features grounded in the texts (self-mention, citation form, hedging) linked to how knowledge is made, not impressions such as 'more scientific'.

topics.name: High-frequency vocabulary base
topics.description: Know, receptively and productively, the most frequent 2,000–3,000 word families of English, with fast, accurate recognition in reading and listening. Because these words make up the large majority of running words in any text, academic texts included, gaps at this level undermine comprehension more than gaps in specialised vocabulary.
masteryEvidence: Recognises high-frequency words quickly in reading and listening, including their common senses
Reaches or approaches mastery on the 1,000–3,000 frequency bands of a vocabulary levels or size test
Uses high-frequency words accurately in speech and writing, including their common alternative meanings
Identifies own gaps in the high-frequency bands from test results and targets them for study
topics.assessmentPrompt: Administer a vocabulary levels test covering the first three 1,000-word bands and check whether any band falls below mastery. Then ask the learner to read a short general-academic passage and summarise it, noting hesitations or misreadings on high-frequency words (e.g. 'state', 'case', 'account') that suggest slow or partial recognition.

topics.name: Lexical coverage and vocabulary size
topics.description: Understand that comprehension depends strongly on the proportion of running words in a text that the reader or listener knows — commonly cited as around 95% for minimal and 98% for comfortable unassisted reading — and use this relationship, with a vocabulary size estimate, to set realistic goals and choose texts. Coverage figures are approximate: comprehension rises gradually with coverage rather than switching on at a threshold, and background knowledge also matters.
masteryEvidence: Explains the relationship between known-word coverage and comprehension, including why one unknown word in 20 feels very different from one in 50
Estimates own coverage of a text by counting unknown words in a sample
Interprets a vocabulary size test result and translates it into realistic reading and listening goals
Recognises that coverage figures are approximate and that background knowledge and text difficulty also affect comprehension
Selects texts at suitable coverage for different purposes (extensive reading versus intensive study)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to count unknown words in a 200-word extract from a set reading and calculate coverage, then say what this implies for how they should read the text and what vocabulary goal follows. Look for correct calculation, a sensible strategy (e.g. pre-learning key terms, using a glossary) and awareness that thresholds are approximate.

topics.name: Word families and derivational morphology
topics.description: Recognise and produce the word-class members of a word family (analyse, analysis, analyst, analytical, analytically) and choose the form a sentence slot requires. Control of derivational morphology multiplies the value of each word learned and prevents a frequent class of errors in academic writing, where nominal and adjectival forms predominate.
masteryEvidence: Produces the noun, verb, adjective and adverb forms of common academic words where they exist
Identifies the word class a sentence slot requires and supplies the correct form
Recognises unstudied family members when reading
Notices and corrects word-form errors in own writing (e.g. 'the analyse of', 'a significance difference')
Recognises family members whose meanings have diverged (e.g. 'critic', 'critique', 'critical', 'criticism')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give eight gapped sentences with a base word in brackets (e.g. 'The ___ of the data took three weeks (analyse)'). Ask the learner to supply the form and name its word class. Check accuracy and whether the learner can explain how the slot signalled the class (e.g. after 'the', before 'of').

topics.name: Academic affixes and Greco-Latin roots
topics.description: Use common academic prefixes (inter-, multi-, sub-, pre-, re-, non-), suffixes (-tion, -ity, -ise/-ize, -ology, -al) and Greco-Latin roots (bio-, geo-, -graph-, -cracy) to infer and remember the meanings of unfamiliar words, while checking inferences, because word parts can mislead (e.g. 'inflammable', 'discursive').
masteryEvidence: Segments unfamiliar academic words into prefix, root and suffix
Uses known affix meanings to propose a plausible meaning, then checks it against context or a dictionary
Explains how a suffix signals word class and how a prefix modifies meaning
Identifies cases where word-part analysis would mislead
Uses word parts as memory links when learning new words
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give six unfamiliar words from academic texts (e.g. 'interdisciplinary', 'decentralisation', 'biodegradable', 'retrospective', plus a misleading one such as 'disinterested'). Ask the learner to segment each, propose a meaning and rate their confidence. Check segmentation, plausibility and whether they flag the misleading item for checking.

topics.name: Core academic vocabulary
topics.description: Recognise and use general academic vocabulary — words such as 'analyse', 'concept', 'significant', 'factor', 'establish' — that recurs across many disciplines and is more frequent in academic than general texts, using lists such as the Academic Word List (AWL) or Academic Vocabulary List (AVL) as starting points while recognising that the frequency, meaning and collocation of listed items vary considerably by discipline.
masteryEvidence: Recognises the meaning of most general academic words met in course readings
Uses general academic words accurately in writing, with appropriate collocates and grammar
Explains how an academic word list was built and what its limitations are (e.g. disciplinary skew, word family versus lemma)
Identifies which listed items are frequent in their own discipline and which are not
Prioritises academic words for study using frequency and relevance to their field
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give 20 AWL/AVL items. Ask the learner to mark those known receptively and productively, write sentences for five, and identify five met in their discipline's readings. Check accurate use (meaning, collocation, word form) and whether the learner can explain why some listed items are rare in their field.

topics.name: Verbs for academic and research processes
topics.description: Control verbs that describe research and reasoning processes — 'investigate', 'examine', 'demonstrate', 'indicate', 'suggest', 'constitute', 'derive', 'attribute' — including their meaning, the strength of claim they convey and their complementation patterns ('attribute X to Y', 'indicate that', 'derive from', 'account for'). These verbs carry much of the propositional and evaluative work of academic writing.
masteryEvidence: Selects a verb that accurately describes a research action (e.g. 'investigate' versus 'measure' versus 'compare')
Distinguishes verbs by claim strength (suggest, indicate, show, demonstrate, prove)
Uses correct complementation patterns (attribute X to Y; consist of; account for; derive from)
Combines process verbs with suitable subjects (e.g. 'the results indicate', 'this study examines')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give gapped sentences describing the methods and findings of a correlational study (e.g. 'The results ___ that…', 'The decline can be ___ to…'). Ask the learner to choose verbs and complete the patterns. Check calibration (no 'prove' for correlational data) and pattern accuracy.

topics.name: Abstract and shell nouns
topics.description: Use abstract nouns ('approach', 'issue', 'factor', 'notion') and shell nouns ('this problem', 'the fact that', 'the claim that', 'the aim is to') that label and encapsulate stretches of text, so that writers can refer back to and characterise ideas, build cohesion and signal stance through the label chosen (a 'finding' versus an 'assumption').
masteryEvidence: Uses 'this/these + shell noun' to refer back to a preceding proposition, choosing a noun that characterises it accurately
Uses shell nouns with their typical complements ('the fact that', 'the aim of this study is to', 'the problem is that')
Chooses labels that convey an appropriate evaluation (claim, finding, assumption, fact)
Avoids vague abstract nouns that leave the referent unclear ('this aspect', 'this thing')
Identifies the antecedent of shell nouns when reading
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a two-sentence passage and ask the learner to begin the next sentence with 'This ___', choosing a noun, then explain the choice. Check that the noun accurately characterises the preceding content and that the learner recognises its stance (e.g. 'this assumption' implies doubt, 'this finding' implies evidence).

topics.name: Technical and discipline-specific terminology
topics.description: Learn field-specific terms as labels for concepts within a disciplinary knowledge structure, understand their precise definitions and relations to other terms, define them on first use where readers may need it, and use them consistently. Technical vocabulary can make up a substantial share of the words in specialised texts, and learning it is inseparable from learning disciplinary content.
masteryEvidence: Identifies technical terms in a disciplinary text and distinguishes them from general academic vocabulary
Explains a term's meaning in relation to neighbouring terms (superordinate, contrasting and component terms)
Defines a key term on first use at a level suited to the reader
Uses a technical term consistently, without unmotivated synonyms
Maintains a personal glossary organised by conceptual relations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a page from a disciplinary textbook. Ask the learner to list the technical terms, group them by conceptual relations and write a one-sentence definition of two. Check whether they separate technical from general academic words and capture how terms relate.

topics.name: Sub-technical vocabulary and polysemy
topics.description: Recognise that many general and academic words take specialised meanings in particular disciplines ('significant' in statistics, 'culture' in biology, 'power' in physics and politics, 'tissue', 'consistent', 'discourse'), and interpret and use the intended sense. Misreading such words is a hidden source of comprehension failure because learners believe they already know them.
masteryEvidence: Identifies words in a disciplinary text whose specialised sense differs from their everyday meaning
Distinguishes the statistical and everyday senses of words such as 'significant', 'random' and 'normal'
Uses the disciplinary sense accurately and avoids ambiguity where both senses are possible
Checks specialised senses in discipline glossaries rather than general dictionaries
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three sentences: 'The difference was not significant (p = .12)'; 'The cells were grown in culture'; 'The results were consistent with previous findings'. Ask the learner to paraphrase each. Check whether they give the specialised senses rather than the everyday ones.

topics.name: Lexical precision and near-synonyms
topics.description: Choose between near-synonyms (affect/effect/impact/influence; show/prove/suggest; method/methodology; increase/rise/growth) by meaning, strength, grammar, collocation and register, so that the chosen word states exactly what the writer intends. Imprecise word choice is a frequent reason markers judge writing unclear or overclaimed.
masteryEvidence: Explains differences within near-synonym sets in terms of meaning, strength, grammar and collocation
Selects the word that fits a specific context and justifies the choice
Corrects confusions such as affect/effect, method/methodology and principal/principle
Uses learner-dictionary or corpus evidence to distinguish near-synonyms
Avoids thesaurus or paraphrasing-tool substitutions that change meaning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sentences, each with three near-synonym options (e.g. 'The findings ___ that the policy had a modest effect': prove/suggest/claim). Ask the learner to choose and justify. Check that justifications refer to meaning, strength or collocation rather than 'it sounds better'.

topics.name: Evaluative vocabulary
topics.description: Use adjectives, adverbs, nouns and verbs that evaluate ideas, evidence and work ('robust', 'compelling', 'limited', 'flawed', 'a shortcoming', 'a strength', 'overlooks', 'convincingly') with appropriate strength and polarity, so that evaluation is precise, justified and suitably mitigated. Evaluative lexis is central to critical writing, where markers expect judgement rather than description.
masteryEvidence: Uses a range of positive and negative evaluative words for evidence, arguments, methods and findings
Grades evaluation by strength (e.g. 'limited', 'weak', 'flawed') to match the case being made
Pairs evaluative words with justification (e.g. 'limited because the sample was self-selected')
Uses evaluative collocations accurately ('robust evidence', 'a compelling argument', 'methodological shortcomings')
Mitigates negative evaluation of published work appropriately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short description of a study with one clear strength and one weakness. Ask the learner to write two evaluative sentences. Check for precise evaluative lexis (not 'good' or 'bad'), calibrated strength, explicit justification and appropriate mitigation of criticism.

topics.name: Multi-word verbs and register
topics.description: Understand phrasal and prepositional verbs ('carry out', 'point out', 'set up', 'come up with', 'look into') in lectures, seminars and texts, and judge in writing when a single-word alternative ('conduct', 'note', 'establish') is more conventional and when the multi-word verb is the normal academic choice ('carry out', 'consist of', 'rule out'). The aim is register judgement, not avoidance: blanket replacement produces stilted prose.
masteryEvidence: Understands common phrasal verbs in lectures and seminar talk, including idiomatic ones
Identifies phrasal verbs in own writing and judges whether a single-word alternative is more appropriate
Uses multi-word verbs that are standard in academic prose ('carry out', 'point out', 'focus on', 'rule out') without needless replacement
Places particles correctly with transitive phrasal verbs, including with pronoun objects
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with six multi-word verbs, three colloquial ('find out', 'go up', 'come up with') and three standard in academic prose ('carry out', 'point out', 'rule out'). Ask for a revision for a report. Check that colloquial verbs are replaced appropriately, standard ones are kept, and the learner can explain the difference.

topics.name: Inferring word meaning from context
topics.description: Infer the meaning of unknown words while reading or listening by using co-text (definitions, examples, contrasts, appositives), word parts and background knowledge, and check the inference against later context or a dictionary when the word matters. Successful inferencing depends on knowing most of the surrounding words, so it complements rather than replaces vocabulary learning.
masteryEvidence: Uses explicit co-text clues (definitions, appositives, 'such as', contrast markers) to infer meaning
Combines word-part and contextual evidence to form a hypothesis about meaning
Checks and revises an inference using later context or a dictionary when the word is important
Decides whether to skip, infer or look up an unknown word according to reading purpose
Reports the evidence behind an inference and a realistic confidence level
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with three unfamiliar words, each supported by a different clue type (definition, contrast, example). Ask the learner to infer each meaning, name the clue used and rate their confidence, then check. Look for evidence-based inferences, realistic confidence and willingness to revise.

topics.name: Using learner and specialist dictionaries
topics.description: Use monolingual learner dictionaries, collocation dictionaries, specialist glossaries and bilingual or bilingualised dictionaries effectively — finding the right entry and sense, and using grammar codes, examples, frequency and register labels — while recognising the risks of taking the first bilingual equivalent or treating machine-translation output as a dictionary.
masteryEvidence: Selects the sense of a polysemous word that fits the context
Uses grammar information (countability, verb patterns) and example sentences to produce correct sentences
Uses a collocation dictionary to find suitable verbs and adjectives for a noun
Cross-checks a bilingual equivalent in a monolingual dictionary or corpus before using it in writing
Uses discipline glossaries or specialist dictionaries for technical terms
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a sentence containing an unfamiliar polysemous word and a short writing task that requires a new verb pattern. Ask the learner to use a learner dictionary for both, thinking aloud. Check sense selection, use of grammar codes and examples, and whether production follows the pattern shown.

topics.name: Deliberate vocabulary learning systems
topics.description: Set up and maintain a system for deliberately learning selected words — paper word cards or spaced-retrieval software recording form, meaning, collocates and an example — and review by retrieval at expanding intervals. Deliberate learning efficiently establishes form–meaning links for priority vocabulary and complements the large amount of exposure needed for depth.
masteryEvidence: Selects words for deliberate study using frequency and relevance criteria
Records each item with form, meaning, collocates and an example from own reading
Practises by retrieval (recalling the word or meaning) rather than rereading lists
Schedules reviews at increasing intervals using software or a manual system
Monitors and adjusts the system, retiring known items and adding productive practice
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show their vocabulary system and explain how they choose words, what they record, and how and when they review. Check for explicit selection criteria, retrieval-based practice, spacing, and information beyond a translation.

topics.name: Moving vocabulary into productive use
topics.description: Develop depth of knowledge of selected words — form, meaning, grammar, collocation, register and constraints on use — so that words recognised in reading and listening can be used accurately in speech and writing, and trial new words in low-stakes production with feedback before relying on them in assessed work.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes words they can recognise from words they can use and selects a manageable number to activate
Gathers productive information for target words (patterns, collocates, register) from texts and dictionaries
Trials target words in speaking and writing and seeks feedback on their use
Uses newly activated words accurately in assessed writing
Avoids using words known only receptively in high-stakes texts until they have been checked
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to choose five words they recognise but do not yet use and to write a short paragraph about their subject using them. Check the accuracy of grammar and collocation, and ask which uses they are confident about and how they checked the others.

topics.name: Word grammar and complementation patterns
topics.description: Know the grammatical patterns that individual verbs, nouns and adjectives take — dependent prepositions ('focus on', 'contribute to', 'an increase in', 'consistent with'), clause complements ('emphasise that', 'aim to', 'an attempt to') and object patterns — and use them accurately. Many errors perceived as 'grammar' in academic writing are word-specific pattern errors.
masteryEvidence: Uses dependent prepositions accurately with common academic verbs, nouns and adjectives
Selects the correct complement type (that-clause, to-infinitive, -ing form, noun phrase) after common verbs and nouns
Records new words together with their patterns
Corrects own pattern errors (e.g. 'discuss about', 'emphasise on', 'consistent to')
Recognises that related words may take different patterns ('emphasise X' but 'put emphasis on X')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give ten sentences mixing pattern errors and correct uses (e.g. 'discuss about', 'contribute to', 'consistent to', 'aim at improving' versus 'aim to improve'). Ask the learner to identify and correct the errors without changing correct items, and to state the pattern for each word.

topics.name: Countability of academic nouns
topics.description: Handle the countability of nouns frequent in academic writing: uncountable nouns whose equivalents are countable in many other languages ('research', 'evidence', 'information', 'knowledge', 'equipment', 'feedback'), nouns with countable and uncountable senses ('theory', 'experience', 'work'), irregular plurals ('criterion/criteria', 'phenomenon/phenomena', 'hypothesis/hypotheses') and the variable treatment of 'data'. Countability errors propagate to articles, quantifiers and agreement.
masteryEvidence: Uses common academic uncountable nouns without plural -s or 'a/an', with suitable quantifiers or countable alternatives ('much research', 'a piece of evidence', 'several studies')
Distinguishes countable and uncountable senses of nouns such as 'theory', 'experience' and 'work'
Uses irregular Greco-Latin plurals correctly
Applies a consistent, field-appropriate treatment of 'data' (plural or mass) within a text
Uses dictionary countability codes to check unfamiliar nouns
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph containing 'researches shows', 'an evidence', 'a criteria', 'many informations' and some correct uses. Ask for corrections. Check accuracy, the knock-on changes to agreement and articles, and whether the learner applies a consistent treatment of 'data'.

topics.name: Spelling conventions and consistency
topics.description: Spell academic vocabulary accurately and consistently: follow one variety (e.g. British or American) or whatever a style guide requires within a text, manage variable spellings such as -ise/-ize, and avoid frequently confused forms (principle/principal, affect/effect, dependent/dependant, licence/license, its/it's). Inconsistent or inaccurate spelling distracts readers and is penalised in many marking criteria.
masteryEvidence: Applies one spelling variety consistently within a text
Sets the spell-checker language to the chosen variety and recognises what it cannot catch
Spells high-frequency academic words accurately, including derived forms (argue/argument, refer/referred)
Distinguishes commonly confused pairs in context
Follows a style guide or module requirement where it specifies spelling
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 120-word paragraph mixing British and American spellings and containing three confusable-word errors. Ask the learner to make it consistently British and correct the errors. Check consistency (including -ise/-ize), accuracy, and whether they notice real-word errors a spell-checker would miss.

topics.name: Vocabulary of university study
topics.description: Understand and use the vocabulary of university study and administration — module, credit, seminar, tutorial, assessment brief, learning outcome, formative and summative assessment, extension, extenuating (mitigating) circumstances, personal tutor, VLE — including institution-specific variants. Misunderstanding these terms can lead to missed deadlines, misdirected requests and lost marks.
masteryEvidence: Explains key terms in their own institution's handbook and assessment documents
Identifies whom to contact for a given issue from institutional role terms (module leader, personal tutor, programme administrator)
Uses institutional terms correctly in emails and requests
Recognises local variants (e.g. 'mitigating' versus 'extenuating circumstances', 'unit' versus 'module')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an extract from a module handbook and ask the learner to explain five terms (e.g. 'formative', 'extension', 'learning outcome', 'credit', 'extenuating circumstances') and what action each might require of them. Check for accurate, institution-specific understanding and its practical implications.

topics.name: Assignment command words
topics.description: Interpret assignment and examination command words — analyse, evaluate, discuss, critically assess, compare, outline, examine, explain, to what extent — in terms of the cognitive operations and text structures they typically require, while recognising that tutors use them inconsistently and that the whole task, criteria and context must be read together.
masteryEvidence: Explains what each common command word typically requires, distinguishing description from analysis and evaluation
Identifies the command word(s), topic and focus in a complex assignment question
Plans an answer structure suited to the command (e.g. an explicit judgement for 'to what extent')
Checks the interpretation against marking criteria and seeks clarification when the task is ambiguous
Recognises implicit commands in questions without a command word (e.g. 'Why did…?', 'Is X justified?')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two questions on one topic: 'Outline the causes of X' and 'To what extent was X caused by Y?'. Ask the learner to explain the difference and sketch a plan for each. Check that the second plan weighs Y against other causes and reaches a judgement, while the first is mainly descriptive.

topics.name: Academic abbreviations and Latin expressions
topics.description: Understand and use common academic abbreviations and Latin expressions (e.g., i.e., et al., cf., etc., vs., viz., ibid., n.d., ca.) correctly in reading and writing, following the conventions of the referencing or style guide in use, and introduce acronyms and initialisms in full on first use.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes 'e.g.' (for example) from 'i.e.' (that is) and uses each correctly
Uses 'et al.' correctly in citations according to the required referencing style
Introduces an acronym in full at first mention and uses it consistently thereafter
Follows style-guide conventions on punctuation and placement (e.g. Latin abbreviations within parentheses in APA style)
Interprets less common abbreviations in sources (cf., viz., ibid.) when reading
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sentences with gaps for 'e.g.', 'i.e.', 'et al.' and 'cf.', and a paragraph that uses an acronym before defining it. Ask the learner to complete and repair them. Check the e.g./i.e. distinction, acronym definition at first mention, and punctuation consistent with the required guide.

dependencies.reason: Most academic collocations combine high-frequency verbs and adjectives (make, take, play, strong, high) with nouns; learners need these words before they can notice how they combine.
Learning specific academic collocations presupposes treating word combinations as units to be noticed and recorded.
Academic collocations are built around general academic nouns, verbs and adjectives (evidence, conduct, significant), which must be known first.
Repairing miscollocations requires knowing the conventional collocates that replace them.
Collocation dictionaries and learner-dictionary examples are the main tools for checking and repairing verb–noun choices independently.
Bundles are recurrent multi-word sequences; learners must already attend to multi-word units to notice them.
Many research-oriented bundles are noun-phrase fragments ending in 'of (the)', whose completion depends on control of postmodification.
Text-oriented bundles must be learned as units with fixed form, which depends on awareness of multi-word units.
Transition and result bundles are multi-word linking adverbials; learners usually meet the logical relations through single-word connectors first.
Stance frames are recurrent multi-word sequences that must be recognised and stored as units.
Most stance bundles are anticipatory-it frames with extraposed that- or to-clauses; without that grammar the frames are produced ungrammatically.
Spoken formulas are processed and produced as prefabricated units, so learners must first attend to multi-word units.
Knowing how academic speech differs from writing explains why these formulas are frequent in lectures but marked in essays.
Fixed expressions lie at the most restricted end of the collocational continuum; the continuum is the framework for understanding their fixedness.
Deciding whether an idiom or binomial suits academic prose is a register judgement that builds on knowing formal-style tendencies.
Concordance lines are only informative to learners who know to look for recurrent co-occurrence patterns.
Learners usually consult dictionaries for usage first; corpus searches extend that reference habit to questions dictionaries do not answer.
Phrasebank entries are largely organising and transition formulas; knowing how these work prevents meaning errors when selecting from lists.
Many phrasebank entries are stance frames; choosing among them requires judging their strength against the evidence.
Phrasebanks are organised by rhetorical function and move; learners need the idea that genres have purposes and moves to use them well.
The spoken–written contrast is a specific case of mode variation; learners need the general idea that situation shapes language before analysing mode in detail.
Lexical density and grammatical intricacy are described by counting clauses and identifying their elements, so learners need basic clause analysis.
Formality features are only meaningful as responses to tenor and mode; without that frame they become an arbitrary list of prohibitions.
Testing prescriptive rules presupposes knowing the conventional features those rules are about (first person, sentence-initial conjunctions, questions).
Choosing impersonal construals requires control of the passive and agent deletion, the main impersonal resource.
Learners who still hold 'never use I' as an absolute rule cannot treat presence as a genuine choice; questioning the rule usually comes first.
Managing density depends on understanding that writing packs meaning into noun phrases while speech spreads it across clauses.
Compressing and unpacking information is largely done by creating and reversing nominalisations.
Many vague items ('stuff', 'a lot of', 'things') are first met as informal features, so formality work usually introduces the problem.
Bounding claims relies on controlled quantifiers (most, some, a minority of, few) in place of 'all', 'everyone' and 'a lot of'.
Learners need to see claims as positions requiring support before they recognise why unbounded generalisations are a weakness rather than a stylistic flourish.
Inclusive wording is a tenor and audience decision; learners need to think about who is addressed and referred to before choosing terms.
Gender-neutral reference (singular 'they', pluralisation) requires secure control of pronoun reference and agreement.
Writing for lay readers depends on the ability to unpack nominalisations and dense noun phrases deliberately.
Writers must recognise which of their terms are technical, and what they mean precisely, before they can replace or gloss them for outsiders.
Lay communication applies general audience-and-purpose analysis to readers whose knowledge and interests differ sharply from the marker's.
Authorial presence versus impersonality is one of the main dimensions on which disciplines differ; learners compare fields along it.
Explaining stylistic differences requires seeing disciplines as communities with shared purposes, genres and ways of validating knowledge.
Hedging, boosting and engagement are compared across fields as metadiscourse resources, so the concept gives learners categories for comparison.
Recognising the different situations of university communication (lectures, seminars, tutorials, VLE forums) provides the situational contrasts register analysis works with.
Coverage is easiest to understand once learners see that a small set of high-frequency families already accounts for most running words.
Choosing the form a slot needs requires identifying the slot's grammatical function (subject head, modifier, adverbial).
Using affixes and roots for inference presupposes knowing how derivational affixes build family members and mark word class.
General academic lists such as the AWL are defined as vocabulary beyond the high-frequency base and are learned and used within high-frequency co-text.
Academic word lists are organised by family or lemma, and using listed words productively depends on choosing the right family member.
Research-process verbs are a semantically defined subset of general academic vocabulary.
Controlling these verbs depends on their complementation patterns (attribute X to Y, indicate that, consist of).
Most shell and abstract nouns (approach, factor, notion, assumption) are general academic vocabulary.
Shell nouns occur in characteristic patterns (N that, N to, the N is that), which build on noun complementation patterns.
Many technical terms, especially in science, medicine and social science, are built from Greco-Latin roots and affixes that aid recognition and recall.
Technical terms label concepts in a knowledge structure; building topic knowledge and learning its terms develop together, with schema support making terms learnable.
Seeing disciplines as communities with shared lexis explains why terms have fixed meanings that must not be paraphrased freely.
Sub-technical items are general or academic words with additional specialised senses; the general sense must be known before the contrast can be drawn.
The idea that fields assign fixed, precise meanings to terms helps learners suspect a specialised sense in familiar-looking words.
Resolving which sense is intended relies on co-text clues and checking, the procedure developed in contextual inferencing.
Most problematic near-synonym sets (affect/impact/influence; method/methodology) are general academic words that must first be known.
Collocation is one of the main criteria distinguishing near-synonyms (have an impact on, exert an influence on).
Learner-dictionary usage notes and examples are a primary tool for distinguishing near-synonyms independently.
Evaluative vocabulary is organised in graded near-synonym sets (limited, weak, flawed); calibrating evaluation requires the ability to distinguish them.
Learners need to understand evaluation as an act distinct from description before a repertoire for expressing it becomes meaningful.
Deciding when to replace a phrasal verb is a register judgement that depends on knowing the tendencies of formal academic style.
Using multi-word verbs accurately involves word-specific patterns: transitivity, particle placement and dependent prepositions.
Inferencing succeeds only when most surrounding words are known; understanding coverage tells learners when to infer and when the text is too dense.
Word-part analysis is one of the main knowledge sources learners combine with co-text when inferring meaning.
World and topic knowledge is a key knowledge source for plausible lexical inferences.
Finding derived forms in a dictionary requires recognising the headword and family relationships.
Word-card and software systems apply retrieval practice and spacing; understanding why these work helps learners use them properly rather than rereading.
Selecting words worth deliberate study depends on understanding frequency and coverage.
Recording form, meaning, collocation and example for each item draws on dictionary information.
Productive use requires knowing the grammatical patterns a word takes, which receptive knowledge often lacks.
Activating a word means using it with its usual collocates, so learners need to attend to co-occurrence.
Words usually enter a learner's productive repertoire after their form–meaning link has been secured through deliberate study.
Patterns are first learned and generalised on frequent verbs and nouns (depend on, interested in, decide to).
Describing complementation (object, complement, prepositional phrase, clause) presupposes basic clause analysis.
The problematic nouns (research, evidence, criterion, phenomenon) are largely general academic vocabulary.
Learner-dictionary countability codes ([C]/[U]) are the main way learners check unfamiliar nouns independently.
Many academic spelling problems arise at morpheme boundaries (suffixation, doubling, -ise/-ize), which depend on understanding derivation.
Terms such as seminar, tutorial and VLE name teaching formats whose expectations differ between education systems.
Most command words are academic process verbs (analyse, examine, evaluate) whose general meanings are learned first.
Command words are met in assessment briefs alongside terms such as learning outcome and criteria, which frame their interpretation.
Learners check expansions and usage of unfamiliar abbreviations in dictionaries and style guides.

guidance.summary: Collocation awareness is a precondition for learning phraseology because learners tend to attend to individual words; Schmidt's noticing hypothesis implies that combinations not noticed are unlikely to be learned. Nesselhauf's analysis of advanced learner writing shows frequent collocation errors, especially with restricted combinations, so awareness is worth building early. Concordance lines make co-occurrence patterns visible efficiently, and Nation's treatment of multiword units supports recording vocabulary in chunks.

activities.title: Chunk hunt
learnerActions: Highlight every combination of two or more words in an academic paragraph that seem to 'go together'
With a partner, agree which are fixed, which are strong preferences and which are free combinations
Add five combinations to your vocabulary record, each with an example sentence
activities.intendedInsight: Many meanings are carried by combinations rather than single words.
activities.rationale: Explicit noticing directs attention to multi-word form–meaning pairings that learners might otherwise process word by word.

activities.title: Concordance noticing
learnerActions: Read 20 concordance lines for a node word such as 'research' or 'evidence'
List the verbs and adjectives that occur with it
Note combinations you expected but did not find (e.g. 'make research') and discuss why
activities.intendedInsight: Collocational preference is conventional, probabilistic and observable in data.
activities.rationale: Concordance displays make recurrent co-occurrence salient, as Hunston describes for corpus-informed language teaching.

difficulties.pattern: 'If each word is correct and the grammar is correct, the phrase must be correct.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Combinations such as 'make research', 'strong rain' or 'big importance' defended as logical.
difficulties.response: Show corpus frequency evidence and explain that collocation is conventional rather than logical. Avoid presenting it as an inaccessible 'native-speaker intuition'; evidence is available to every learner.

difficulties.pattern: Vocabulary recorded as single-word translation pairs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Word lists with only L1 equivalents and no collocates or examples.
difficulties.response: Model records that include collocates and example sentences, and set notebook tasks that require them.

diagnostic.task: Ask which verb goes with each noun: ___ a conclusion, ___ research, ___ a question, ___ a role.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives 'draw/reach', 'conduct/carry out/do', 'raise/pose/address' and 'play', and notes that more than one verb can be possible with different meanings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct for some nouns, with transferred choices for others (e.g. 'make research').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses 'make' or 'do' throughout and sees no difference.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation, introduce collocation through high-frequency nouns in course texts and simple recording formats. Pre-sessional and UG courses can introduce concordance lines and collocation dictionaries as tools.

guidance.summary: Ackermann and Chen's Academic Collocation List offers a corpus-derived, expert-judged inventory of academic collocations that can serve as a syllabus starting point. Durrant and Schmitt's comparison of native and non-native writers suggests learners rely on frequent, general combinations and underuse strongly associated but less frequent ones, so teaching should extend range, not just correct errors. As with single-word lists, disciplinary relevance should be checked against field texts.

activities.title: Collocation grids
learnerActions: Choose eight nouns central to your field
Use an academic collocation list or corpus to find common verbs and adjectives for each
Build a grid showing which combinations occur and tick those you have met in your reading
Write a short paragraph using six of the combinations
activities.intendedInsight: Each academic noun brings a limited set of conventional verbs and adjectives.
activities.rationale: The ACL was designed as a pedagogical inventory of academic collocations; grids turn it into a production resource tied to the learner's field.

activities.title: Upgrade the collocation
learnerActions: Highlight adjective–noun and verb–noun combinations in your draft
For each very general combination ('big problem', 'get results'), find a more precise academic alternative
Check each alternative in a corpus or collocation dictionary before using it
activities.intendedInsight: Collocational range adds precision and makes writing easier for expert readers to process.
activities.rationale: Durrant and Schmitt found non-native writers relied on frequent collocations and underused strongly associated ones; this activity targets that gap.

difficulties.pattern: Overuse of a few safe combinations ('play an important role', 'have a big impact').
difficulties.revealedBy: The same small set of collocations repeated across texts.
difficulties.response: Extend range by recording alternatives and their meaning differences. Do not ban frequent collocations; they are correct and useful.

difficulties.pattern: List items used without regard to meaning or field.
difficulties.revealedBy: Combinations such as 'conduct a conclusion' or 'empirical opinion'.
difficulties.response: Teach collocations in context with examples and have learners check items in disciplinary texts.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to complete 'The study ___ a significant ___ between the two groups' and give alternatives.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives 'found/revealed/identified … difference' with alternatives and notes any restrictions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct core collocation but few alternatives, or one miscollocation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses inappropriate verbs and nouns ('made a significant change').

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional teaching can draw on the ACL and course readings. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, focus on collocations of key disciplinary nouns, checked against field texts.
reviewNotes: durrantschmitt2009 is a proposed reference; ackermannchen2013 and nesselhauf2003 independently support the topic framing.

guidance.summary: Nesselhauf and Laufer and Waldman both found verb–noun collocation errors to be frequent and persistent, even at advanced levels, and attributed many of them to the learner's L1, where a combination that works in the L1 is carried over into English. Because such errors resist general exposure, individual error records combined with resource checking are likely to work better than generic lists. Contrastive comparison with the L1 can help when used as a learner strategy rather than as a teacher's assumption about a group; Granger's learner-corpus approach shows how to compare learner and expert use systematically.

activities.title: Personal miscollocation log
learnerActions: Collect verb–noun errors marked in recent feedback
Look up each noun in a collocation dictionary and record the conventional verbs
Note whether each error came from a word-for-word translation
Before submitting your next assignment, search your draft for those nouns
activities.intendedInsight: My collocation errors are patterned and checkable.
activities.rationale: Laufer and Waldman found that collocation errors persist at advanced proficiency and that many reflect L1 influence, which suggests targeted individual checking rather than relying on exposure alone.

activities.title: Congruent or not?
learnerActions: Translate ten English verb–noun collocations into your L1 word for word
Identify which have direct equivalents and which do not
Concentrate practice on the combinations that differ
activities.intendedInsight: Combinations that differ from the L1 are the ones most worth deliberate attention.
activities.rationale: Nesselhauf found L1 influence to be a major factor in learners' collocation errors, so contrasting with the L1 targets the highest-risk items.

difficulties.pattern: Word-for-word transfer of L1 verb–noun combinations.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors concentrated in combinations whose L1 equivalent uses a different verb (e.g. the L1 verb meaning 'make' used with 'research').
difficulties.response: Use contrastive learner-led activities and collocation dictionaries. Do not assume all speakers of a language make the same errors; work from each learner's texts.

difficulties.pattern: Confusion among delexical verbs (make, do, have, take).
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Do a mistake', 'make progress' and 'do progress' alternating in the same text.
difficulties.response: Teach delexical verbs with their nouns in sets and accept legitimate variation between varieties of English (e.g. 'take/make a decision').

difficulties.pattern: Transitive and intransitive pairs confused (raise/rise).
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Rise a question', 'prices were raised by 5%' used to mean prices went up.
difficulties.response: Teach the pair as a contrast in verb pattern (object or no object) with academic nouns.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to correct and explain: 'In this essay I will make a research on how temperature raises crop yields.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Corrects to 'conduct/carry out research' (uncountable, no article) and checks whether 'raises' or 'increases' with the right subject is meant, explaining both collocation and countability.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects only one of the problems.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no error.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce error logs and collocation dictionaries. In-sessional and PGR support works best on learners' own drafts, where persistent individual errors can be targeted before submission or publication.

guidance.summary: Hyland's functional taxonomy of bundles (research-, text- and participant-oriented) and his evidence that research-oriented bundles are especially frequent in science and engineering writing illustrate both the usefulness of bundles and their disciplinary skew. Cortes found that student writers rarely used the bundles found in published texts in their discipline, and used them differently when they did. Because bundles are often structurally incomplete (many end in 'of the'), they should be taught with their typical grammatical continuations and in context.

activities.title: Bundles in context
learnerActions: Find six research-oriented bundles in a published article from your field
Copy the full sentence for each
Mark what follows each bundle (noun phrase, clause)
Write your own sentences using the same frames
activities.intendedInsight: Bundles are frames with predictable grammatical continuations.
activities.rationale: Bundles are frequently structurally incomplete, so learners need to observe their continuations; Hyland's study shows which types cluster in which disciplines.

activities.title: Student versus expert
learnerActions: Compare the bundles in a high-scoring student assignment and a published article in the same field
List bundles that appear only in the published article
Choose three to try in your next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: Novice and expert writers in the same field use different bundles.
