guidance.summary: Chung and Nation found that technical vocabulary accounts for a substantial share of running words in specialised texts and proposed ways of identifying it; Woodward-Kron argues that specialist language is 'more than jargon': learning terms is learning concepts and how they relate. EAP teachers rarely have content expertise, so the most productive approach is to equip learners with methods (concept-mapped glossaries, attention to definitions in texts) and to collaborate with subject staff.

activities.title: Concept-mapped glossary
learnerActions: Extract technical terms from a chapter
Map their relationships (is a type of, is part of, causes, contrasts with)
Write a definition of each in the pattern term – class – distinguishing features
Check definitions against a textbook glossary or with a subject tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Technical terms make sense within a network of concepts.
activities.rationale: Woodward-Kron shows that technical language encodes disciplinary knowledge structures, so learning terms relationally supports learning content.

activities.title: Technical or not?
learnerActions: Rate words in a specialised text from 'general' to 'highly technical'
Compare ratings with a partner and discuss disagreements
Check doubtful items in a specialist dictionary
activities.intendedInsight: Technicality is a continuum, not a yes/no category.
activities.rationale: Chung and Nation used a rating scale to identify technical vocabulary; this activity adapts the approach for learners.

difficulties.pattern: An L1 equivalent term with different scope is assumed to match the English term.
difficulties.revealedBy: Terms used with a broader or narrower meaning than the field intends, often where the L1 term covers a different conceptual range.
difficulties.response: Compare definitions explicitly and use specialist bilingual glossaries with caution, checking English definitions.

difficulties.pattern: Varying technical terms to avoid repetition.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Participants', 'subjects', 'respondents' and 'students' alternating for one group.
difficulties.response: Explain that in academic writing changing a term signals a change of referent; keep key terms constant.

difficulties.pattern: Definitions memorised without conceptual understanding.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate textbook definitions recited, but terms misapplied in new examples.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to apply terms to new cases and explain relations between terms.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to define a key term from their field and explain how it differs from a closely related term.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate definition with class and distinguishing features, and a clear contrast with the neighbouring term.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate definition but a weak or confused contrast.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot define or confuses the terms.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation, terminology is met in subject-content modules and benefits from joint planning with content tutors. Pre-sessional courses with ESAP strands can build glossaries from departmental texts. In UG, PGT and PGR settings, work is best embedded with subject staff; PGR writers may also need to define or coin terms in their own research.
reviewNotes: chungnation2003 and woodwardkron2008 are proposed references; nation2013 independently supports the general framing.
Overlaps with coh.terminological-consistency (consistent use across a text) and fun.defining (definition structures); both could take this topic as a prerequisite.

guidance.summary: Hyland and Tse demonstrate that items on general academic word lists often have different meanings and collocations in different disciplines, which challenges the idea that a single meaning can be taught for each. Because learners believe they know these words, misinterpretations go unnoticed; quick paraphrase tasks are an efficient way to surface them. Nation's account of specialised vocabulary supports anchoring teaching in disciplinary texts, ideally with input from subject staff.

activities.title: Familiar words, special meanings
learnerActions: Read sentences from texts in your field containing familiar words (e.g. significant, culture, power, normal)
Paraphrase each sentence
Compare your paraphrases with the disciplinary meaning given by a glossary or tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Words I think I know may carry a different meaning in my field.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse's evidence of discipline-specific meanings shows why familiar-looking words need checking in context.

activities.title: Two-sense sentences
learnerActions: Write two sentences for each target word, one with the everyday sense and one with the disciplinary sense
Swap with a partner, who identifies which is which
Discuss contexts where a reader could misinterpret the word
activities.intendedInsight: Context determines sense, and ambiguity can be avoided by wording.
activities.rationale: Producing both senses contrastively makes the distinction explicit, supporting the recognition of specialised senses that Nation describes.

difficulties.pattern: 'I know this word', so the everyday meaning is applied.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paraphrases that give the everyday sense of 'significant', 'culture' or 'consistent'.
difficulties.response: Use short paraphrase checks on set readings to surface misreadings, and keep a list of discipline-specific senses.

difficulties.pattern: 'Significant' used to mean 'important' in quantitative reports.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'There was a significant difference' with no statistical test reported.
difficulties.response: Teach alternatives ('substantial', 'notable', 'important') and reserve 'significant' for statistical significance in quantitative fields.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what 'The effect was not significant' means in a psychology results section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the result did not reach statistical significance at the chosen level, not that it was unimportant.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions statistics vaguely but also equates it with 'not important'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Interprets it as 'not important'.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, raise awareness with cross-disciplinary examples. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, build discipline-specific lists from set readings, ideally with subject staff.
reviewNotes: Classified as ESAP because the specialised senses are discipline-bound, though the awareness itself can be taught generically.
The skeleton's own example of statistical 'significant' overlaps with num.statistical-vocabulary.

guidance.summary: Corpus comparison of near-synonyms reveals differences in collocation, grammar and evaluative connotation that dictionaries may not capture, as Hunston shows, and Hinkel documents L2 writers' reliance on a narrow range of general vocabulary that reduces precision. Teach in contrastive sets drawn from learners' own texts, using learner dictionaries and concordances as evidence. Swales and Feak's attention to precise word choice in graduate writing offers models.

activities.title: Near-synonym investigation
learnerActions: Choose a set such as affect/influence/impact
Compare 20 concordance lines for each
Record differences in grammar (verb or noun), collocates and typical subjects
Write a short usage guide for classmates
activities.intendedInsight: Near-synonyms differ systematically in grammar and collocation.
activities.rationale: Hunston shows how corpus comparison reveals usage differences between near-synonyms.

activities.title: Thesaurus trap
learnerActions: Run a paragraph through a thesaurus or paraphrasing tool
Identify substitutions that change meaning, strength or register
Restore or improve each with a justified choice
activities.intendedInsight: Synonyms are rarely interchangeable in context.
activities.rationale: Hinkel's work on L2 academic vocabulary highlights restricted range and imprecise substitution; examining tool output makes the risks concrete.

difficulties.pattern: Synonyms treated as interchangeable.
difficulties.revealedBy: Thesaurus or paraphrasing-tool substitutions that distort meaning ('the study proves' changed to 'the study confirms').
difficulties.response: Require a justification for each substitution and check it in a learner dictionary or corpus.

difficulties.pattern: Strength miscalibrated through verb or adjective choice.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Prove' for suggestive evidence; 'huge' for modest differences.
difficulties.response: Link word choice to the evidence and teach graded sets.

difficulties.pattern: Confusion of similar forms (affect/effect, principal/principle).
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in fluent writing that the learner can correct when prompted.
difficulties.response: Add the pairs to a proofreading checklist. Do not reteach the distinction if the learner can already explain it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain the difference between 'method' and 'methodology', and between 'affect' and 'impact', with examples.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Distinguishes procedure from rationale/study of methods, and explains grammatical and collocational differences between 'affect' (verb) and 'impact' (noun, and verb in some varieties).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains one pair accurately.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats both pairs as equivalent.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, target common confusion sets. In UG, PGT and PGR settings, work from the learner's own drafts and disciplinary near-synonym sets.

guidance.summary: Hunston and Thompson's work on evaluation shows that evaluative meaning is spread across lexis and grammar, and Martin and White's Appraisal framework offers categories — appreciation of things, judgement of people, graduation of strength — that help learners organise evaluative vocabulary. Novice writers often evaluate with a narrow range of general words (good, bad, interesting) or avoid evaluation. Build graded sets organised by what is evaluated (evidence, method, argument) and always pair evaluation with reasons.

activities.title: Evaluation ladders
learnerActions: Build graded sets of evaluative words for evidence (e.g. inconclusive, limited, adequate, strong, compelling)
Do the same for methods and arguments
Use the ladders to evaluate two studies you have read, giving a reason for each judgement
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluation is graded, and strength should match the reasons given.
activities.rationale: The graduation and attitude categories of the Appraisal framework provide a principled way to organise evaluative vocabulary.

activities.title: Evaluation in reviews
learnerActions: Highlight evaluative words in a published book review or article critique
Classify each as positive or negative and note how criticism is softened
Write a short critique of a reading using similar resources
activities.intendedInsight: Expert evaluation is specific, justified and often mitigated.
activities.rationale: Hunston and Thompson show evaluation is pervasive in academic texts and realised through varied lexical resources.

difficulties.pattern: Generic evaluation ('good', 'bad', 'interesting').
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques built on a handful of general adjectives.
difficulties.response: Build graded, object-specific sets and model their use.

difficulties.pattern: 'Who am I to criticise a published expert?'
difficulties.revealedBy: Purely descriptive critiques; criticism hidden or omitted.
difficulties.response: Present mitigated critique as an expected practice and model the language for it.

difficulties.pattern: Strong evaluation without justification.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'This study is useless', 'a perfect theory'.
difficulties.response: Require a reason for each evaluation and calibrate strength to it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to evaluate a study that used a sample of 20 volunteers from one university.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses precise, calibrated evaluation (e.g. 'the small, self-selected sample limits generalisability') with a reason and possibly mitigation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the problem but uses general or over-strong language ('bad sample').
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the study without evaluating it.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, build core evaluative sets. In UG and PGT settings, apply them to critiques and literature reviews. PGR writers refine evaluation of others' work in literature reviews, peer reviews and responses to reviewers.
reviewNotes: Overlaps with sta.attitude-markers and sta.evaluating-others-language; this topic is the lexical repertoire, which those topics could take as a prerequisite.

guidance.summary: Corpus grammar shows that phrasal verbs are far more frequent in conversation and fiction than in academic prose, but Biber's study of university registers shows they are pervasive in classroom teaching, so learners need them receptively. Gardner and Davies show that a relatively small number of lexical verbs and particles account for a large share of phrasal-verb use, supporting a prioritised list. In writing, the teaching point is judgement: some multi-word verbs are entirely standard in academic prose.

activities.title: Lecture phrasal verb log
learnerActions: Note phrasal verbs heard in two lectures or recorded talks
Check meanings in a learner dictionary
Mark which you would use in writing and which only in speech
activities.intendedInsight: Phrasal verbs are common in academic speech even when less common in academic writing.
activities.rationale: Biber's corpus of university registers shows classroom teaching shares many lexical features with conversation, including multi-word verbs.

activities.title: Keep, change or check
learnerActions: Highlight multi-word verbs in your draft
Label each 'keep', 'change' or 'check'
Check doubtful items in an academic corpus or learner dictionary register labels
Revise and justify each change
activities.intendedInsight: Some multi-word verbs belong in academic writing; others have more conventional single-word alternatives.
activities.rationale: Corpus evidence on register distribution lets learners make item-by-item decisions instead of applying a blanket rule.

difficulties.pattern: 'All phrasal verbs are informal.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Contorted replacements ('executed the experiment', 'the sample was comprised of') and avoidance of standard verbs such as 'carry out'.
difficulties.response: Show corpus evidence that some multi-word verbs are normal in academic prose. Do not teach a blanket replacement list.

difficulties.pattern: Particle meanings opaque, so phrasal verbs are avoided in listening and speaking.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension breakdowns in lectures, especially for learners whose L1 typically expresses such meanings with single verbs rather than verb + particle combinations.
difficulties.response: Teach frequent particles' core meanings (e.g. 'out' as completion or revealing) and high-frequency combinations in context.

difficulties.pattern: Particle placement errors with pronoun objects.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'They pointed out it', 'we will carry out them'.
difficulties.response: Teach the separable pattern with pronouns as a word-grammar rule.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to revise 'We found out that prices went up a lot after the policy was brought in' for a report.
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'We found that prices rose substantially after the policy was introduced', changing colloquial items while keeping clarity.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Changes some items but leaves others or over-formalises.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No changes or meaning distorted.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, emphasise recognition in lectures and basic register judgement. In UG in-sessional work, apply judgement in the student's own drafts and disciplinary genres.
reviewNotes: gardnerdavies2007 is a proposed reference; biber1999lgswe and biber2006 independently support the register claims.

guidance.summary: Nassaji found that L2 learners' lexical inferences were often unsuccessful and that success was associated with the quality of strategy use — especially evaluating and verifying hypotheses — and with drawing on appropriate knowledge sources, rather than with the sheer frequency of strategy use. Coverage research (Hu and Nation) implies that inferencing works best when unknown words are sparse. Teach a short explicit procedure (look for clues, hypothesise, check) and practise with texts at suitable coverage.

activities.title: Clue types
learnerActions: Find unfamiliar words in a short academic text
Classify the clue that helps with each (definition, example, contrast, apposition, word parts, topic knowledge)
Infer each meaning and check it in a dictionary
activities.intendedInsight: Different clues give different kinds and strengths of evidence.
activities.rationale: Nation describes the clue types and steps of guessing from context as a teachable strategy.

activities.title: Think-aloud inferencing
learnerActions: In pairs, read a paragraph and take turns thinking aloud about one unknown word
Name the knowledge source used and the hypothesis
Verify the hypothesis against the next sentences or a dictionary and discuss what worked
activities.intendedInsight: Checking a guess is as important as making it.
activities.rationale: Nassaji found that verifying and evaluating inferences was associated with greater success than simply generating guesses.

difficulties.pattern: Wild guesses from a single clue, never checked.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident but wrong meanings that persist into notes and summaries.
difficulties.response: Require a stated clue and a check for important words.

difficulties.pattern: Every unknown word looked up, so reading is slow and fragmented.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who read with a translation tool open and stop at every unfamiliar word.
difficulties.response: Teach decisions about which words matter for the reading purpose; practise skipping and inferring on texts at high coverage.

difficulties.pattern: 'I should be able to guess everything from context.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Frustration and failure with texts containing many unknown words.
difficulties.response: Explain the link between coverage and inferencing success and recommend pre-learning key terms for dense texts.

diagnostic.task: Give: 'Unlike earlier, more ephemeral studies, this project followed participants for twenty years.' Ask what 'ephemeral' probably means and how the learner knows.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Infers 'short-lived' from the contrast with 'twenty years' and 'unlike', and suggests checking.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a vaguely negative meaning without using the contrast.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot infer or guesses at random.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, practise with graded or accessible texts. In UG in-sessional work, apply the procedure to disciplinary readings, combined with glossary use for technical terms.

guidance.summary: Nation treats dictionary use as a skill to be taught, including choosing the right sense and using dictionaries for production as well as comprehension. Bilingual dictionaries are valuable for speed and comprehension, but production benefits from monolingual entries with grammar information and examples. Machine translation and AI tools now serve as de facto dictionaries, so learners need strategies to check their output against reliable entries.

activities.title: Right sense
learnerActions: Look up polysemous words from a reading (e.g. 'state', 'case', 'issue')
Choose the sense that fits the context and explain your choice
Write a new sentence using the same sense
activities.intendedInsight: The first sense listed is often not the one needed.
activities.rationale: Nation identifies sense selection as a core, teachable dictionary skill.

activities.title: Bilingual to monolingual cross-check
learnerActions: Find an English equivalent for an L1 word you need for an assignment
Check the equivalent in a monolingual learner dictionary and a collocation dictionary
Write a sentence that follows the grammar and collocations shown, then compare with your first attempt
activities.intendedInsight: A translation equivalent is a starting point, not a guarantee of correct use.
activities.rationale: Webb and Nation describe dictionaries as tools for learning use information, not only meaning.

difficulties.pattern: The first sense listed is taken regardless of context.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misinterpretations of polysemous words in notes and summaries.
difficulties.response: Practise reading all senses and matching them to context.

difficulties.pattern: Bilingual equivalents used in writing with L1 grammar and collocation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct word, wrong pattern ('discuss about', 'make research') traceable to the L1 equivalent's behaviour.
difficulties.response: Teach the cross-check routine and the use of example sentences before production.

difficulties.pattern: Grammar codes and examples ignored.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners who use dictionaries only for translation and cannot interpret [U] or 'V that' codes.
difficulties.response: Teach the codes explicitly using the learners' own dictionary.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to use a learner dictionary to decide whether 'advice' can be plural and which preposition follows 'emphasis'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Finds that 'advice' is uncountable ('a piece of advice') and that 'emphasis' takes 'on', citing the entry.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds one answer or cannot locate the grammar information.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Relies on intuition or translation only.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, teach learner-dictionary features explicitly. In UG in-sessional settings, add specialist glossaries and collocation resources relevant to the discipline.
reviewNotes: No listed source reports recent empirical work on learners' use of online dictionaries, machine translation or AI tools as dictionaries; claims about these are practitioner judgement.

guidance.summary: Nation and Webb and Nation argue that deliberate learning with word cards or software is an efficient way to establish form–meaning links, provided it involves retrieval and spacing. Research on the testing effect (Roediger and Karpicke) and distributed practice (Cepeda et al.) explains why retrieval and expanding intervals outperform rereading. Deliberate learning should be balanced with meaning-focused input and output so that words learned on cards are also met and used in context.

activities.title: Build your deck
learnerActions: Choose 20 priority words from your reading using frequency and relevance
Make cards with the word on one side and meaning, collocates and an example on the other
Review by recalling before turning over, at increasing intervals over two weeks
activities.intendedInsight: Retrieval at spaced intervals makes words stick.
activities.rationale: Webb and Nation describe word-card learning with retrieval and spacing as an efficient deliberate learning technique.

activities.title: Retrieval versus rereading
learnerActions: Split ten new words into two sets
Study one set by rereading and the other by self-testing
Test yourself on both sets a week later and compare results
activities.intendedInsight: Self-testing feels harder but produces better retention.
activities.rationale: The testing effect and distributed-practice research show retrieval and spacing benefit long-term retention; a small personal experiment makes this tangible.

difficulties.pattern: Long lists reread rather than retrieved.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report hours of 'learning' with little retention.
difficulties.response: Demonstrate retrieval practice and track results.

difficulties.pattern: Too many words collected, then the system is abandoned.
difficulties.revealedBy: Decks of hundreds of cards with overdue reviews.
difficulties.response: Set realistic daily limits and prioritise by frequency and relevance.

difficulties.pattern: Only the L1 translation is recorded.
difficulties.revealedBy: Cards without collocates or examples; known words misused in writing.
difficulties.response: Add collocation and example fields for words intended for productive use.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe exactly what they did the last time they studied vocabulary.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes selection, retrieval-based practice and a review schedule.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses cards or an app but rereads or reviews irregularly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Rereads lists or has no system.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, set up systems explicitly and check them. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, focus on maintaining systems alongside heavy reading loads and on discipline-relevant selection.
reviewNotes: The cited retrieval and spacing studies are not all vocabulary-specific; their application to L2 word learning is supported by vocabulary researchers but effect sizes may differ.

guidance.summary: Nation's framework of word knowledge distinguishes receptive and productive knowledge of form, meaning and use, and Schmitt's review shows that productive knowledge typically lags behind receptive knowledge and needs additional, targeted practice. Paquot's analysis of learner academic writing shows that even advanced learners underuse or misuse academic vocabulary in production. Activating vocabulary requires gathering use information and trialling words with feedback, not just more exposure.

activities.title: Activate five
learnerActions: Choose five words you recognise but have never used
Collect two authentic examples of each from your reading
Use each in speech (a seminar or study group) and in a paragraph
Ask for feedback and note corrections
activities.intendedInsight: Productive use needs deliberate trialling and feedback.
activities.rationale: Nation's distinction between receptive and productive knowledge implies that production requires additional, use-focused learning.

activities.title: Use-information profile
learnerActions: For a target word, record its patterns, collocates, register and any restrictions from dictionary and corpus evidence
Write three sentences that test different patterns
Peer-check and revise
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing a word productively means knowing how it behaves.
activities.rationale: Schmitt's review stresses multiple dimensions of word knowledge and the need for explicit attention to them.

difficulties.pattern: A newly met word is used in an essay before its behaviour is known.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambitious vocabulary with pattern or collocation errors.
difficulties.response: Encourage trialling in low-stakes writing first and checking patterns. Do not discourage risk-taking itself.

difficulties.pattern: Reliance on a small set of safe, familiar words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive vocabulary in writing despite good reading comprehension.
difficulties.response: Set small activation goals and reward accurate new use.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to use 'constitute' and 'attribute' in sentences about their field.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate sentences with correct patterns ('X constitutes Y'; 'attribute X to Y').
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct meaning, pattern errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot use the words, or meaning errors.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can build activation routines. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, focus on discipline-relevant vocabulary in the learner's own assignments.
reviewNotes: paquot2010 is a proposed reference; nation2013 and schmitt2008 independently support the topic framing.

guidance.summary: Pattern grammar (Hunston and Francis) shows that words have characteristic patterns and that words sharing a pattern often share aspects of meaning, which offers an efficient way to teach and learn them in groups. Corpus grammar documents verb complementation and preposition choice in detail. Treat pattern errors as gaps in lexical knowledge, recorded word by word, rather than as general grammar errors.

activities.title: Pattern families
learnerActions: Group academic verbs by pattern (V that: argue, suggest, indicate; V to-inf: aim, attempt, fail; V n to n: attribute, relate)
Notice meaning similarities within each group
Write sentences using two verbs from each group
activities.intendedInsight: Patterns and meanings go together, so words can be learned in groups.
activities.rationale: Hunston and Francis show that words sharing a pattern tend to share meaning, making pattern-based grouping efficient.

activities.title: Concordance pattern check
learnerActions: Choose three words you are unsure about (e.g. impact, consistent, emphasis)
Look at 20 concordance lines for each
Record the dominant pattern and correct your draft
activities.intendedInsight: Corpus evidence resolves pattern doubts quickly.
activities.rationale: Hunston describes how concordances reveal lexically specific patterns.

difficulties.pattern: Prepositions carried over from the L1 equivalent ('discuss about', 'emphasise on').
difficulties.revealedBy: Pattern errors where the L1 equivalent verb takes a preposition or particle.
difficulties.response: Record words with patterns and use contrastive noticing of high-risk items.

difficulties.pattern: Pattern borrowed from a related word ('emphasise on' from 'emphasis on'; 'discuss about' from 'talk about').
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors that mirror a related word's pattern.
difficulties.response: Contrast related forms explicitly.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to correct 'This essay will discuss about the impact to employment and emphasise on the need for policy.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'discuss the impact on employment and emphasise the need for policy', with explanation of each pattern.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects one or two.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no errors.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, focus on high-frequency patterns. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, target persistent errors in the learner's own writing.
reviewNotes: hunstonfrancis2000 is a proposed reference; hunston2002 and biber1999lgswe independently support the topic.

guidance.summary: Countability in English is partly conceptual and partly lexical convention, so academic nouns whose equivalents are countable in other languages cause persistent errors. Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman describe the count/non-count distinction and its interaction with articles and quantifiers, and corpus grammar shows how countability interacts with determiners. Teach the small set of high-frequency academic uncountables explicitly, with their quantifiers and countable alternatives ('studies', 'findings', 'a piece of evidence').

activities.title: Uncountable alternatives
learnerActions: List the uncountable academic nouns you use most (research, evidence, information, knowledge, feedback)
For each, find a countable alternative or a quantifier phrase (studies, findings, a piece of evidence)
Rewrite sentences from your draft using them
activities.intendedInsight: Countable alternatives let me count what an uncountable noun cannot.
activities.rationale: Hinkel recommends explicit work on high-frequency academic nouns that cause countability errors in L2 writing.

activities.title: The 'data' decision
learnerActions: Check how your required style guide treats 'data'
Count 'data is' and 'data are' in five articles from your field
Decide on one treatment and apply it consistently in your draft
activities.intendedInsight: Some countability questions are style choices requiring consistency rather than errors.
activities.rationale: Style guides differ on 'data' (APA treats it as plural), so learners need to apply a consistent, field-appropriate choice.

difficulties.pattern: Plural or indefinite forms of uncountable nouns ('researches', 'an evidence', 'informations').
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors concentrated in nouns whose equivalents are countable in the learner's L1.
difficulties.response: Teach countable alternatives and quantifiers; check nouns with dictionary codes.

difficulties.pattern: Greco-Latin plurals used as singular ('a criteria', 'this phenomena').
difficulties.revealedBy: Agreement errors with these nouns.
difficulties.response: Teach singular/plural pairs explicitly and practise agreement.

difficulties.pattern: 'Data is' and 'data are' mixed within one text.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistency the learner can fix when it is pointed out.
difficulties.response: Add the item to a proofreading checklist.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to correct 'Many researches has shown that this criteria provide an useful evidence.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'Much research has shown / Many studies have shown that these criteria provide useful evidence', with explanations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrects some errors but not agreement or articles.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees few or no errors.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, target the core uncountables and plurals. In UG and PGT in-sessional work, focus on persistent errors and the 'data' convention in the learner's field.
reviewNotes: Use of 'data' as a singular mass noun is widespread and accepted in many contexts; present it as a style choice to be applied consistently.

guidance.summary: Nation includes written form as one aspect of knowing a word; the spelling of academic words, including derived forms, deserves explicit attention. Consistency often matters more to markers than which variety is chosen: APA style follows American spelling, while many UK institutions accept either variety if it is used consistently. Spell-checkers help but miss real-word errors such as 'principle' for 'principal'.

activities.title: Variety consistency check
learnerActions: Set your word processor's language to the required variety
Search your draft for -ize/-ise, -or/-our and -er/-re forms
Make all instances consistent with your chosen variety or style guide
activities.intendedInsight: Consistency is checkable and mostly mechanical.
activities.rationale: Style guides specify spelling conventions; a targeted search makes consistency manageable.

activities.title: Personal confusables list
learnerActions: Collect spelling and confusable-word errors from your marked work
Group them (suffix changes, confusable pairs, variety mixing)
Search for these items before submitting your next assignment
activities.intendedInsight: My spelling errors are patterned and predictable.
activities.rationale: Treating written form as part of word knowledge supports targeted practice on known weak points.

difficulties.pattern: Varieties mixed because sources and tools use different conventions.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Analyse' and 'analyze', 'behaviour' and 'behavior' in one text.
difficulties.response: Set tools correctly and run a final consistency search.

difficulties.pattern: Real-word errors that spell-checkers do not flag.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Principle investigator', 'it's findings', 'dependant variable' in some fields.
difficulties.response: Add a personal confusables list to proofreading.

difficulties.pattern: Spelling by sound, with errors in vowels, double consonants and silent letters.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors that reflect pronunciation, especially for learners whose L1 has a more transparent sound–spelling relationship or a different writing system.
difficulties.response: Teach morphological spelling patterns (refer/referred, necessary) and frequent irregular forms.

diagnostic.task: Give a sentence with 'analyze', 'behaviour', 'principle investigator' and 'it's results' and ask the learner to correct it for a UK assignment.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Makes the spellings consistently British, corrects 'principal' and 'its', and explains each change.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Fixes variety or confusables, not both.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no problems.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, establish the habit of consistency and checking. In UG in-sessional settings, align with departmental and style-guide requirements.
reviewNotes: Few listed sources address spelling in EAP specifically; guidance draws on general vocabulary research and style-guide practice.

guidance.summary: Institutional vocabulary is part of the tacit knowledge that students new to an education system must acquire. Language socialisation research (Duff) treats such learning as part of joining an academic community, and Wingate argues that academic expectations should be made explicit for all students rather than left to be absorbed. Terminology differs between institutions and countries, so teaching should use learners' own institutional documents.

activities.title: Handbook treasure hunt
learnerActions: Use your programme or module handbook to find the meaning of ten key terms
For each, write what you would need to do (e.g. how to apply for an extension)
Compare with a partner and list remaining questions for your tutor
activities.intendedInsight: Institutional terms have practical consequences that I can find out about.
activities.rationale: Making institutional expectations explicit through authentic documents supports inclusive access, as Wingate argues.

activities.title: Who do I ask?
learnerActions: Read short scenarios (illness before a deadline, a question about a mark, a timetable clash)
Identify the relevant procedure and role (module leader, personal tutor, student services)
Draft the first sentence of an email using the correct terms
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing roles and procedures helps me act appropriately.
activities.rationale: Socialisation into an academic community includes learning its roles and practices through participation and explicit guidance.

difficulties.pattern: Terms assumed to mean what they meant in a previous system ('tutorial', 'course', 'college', 'assignment').
difficulties.revealedBy: Misunderstanding of what a tutorial involves or of what 'course' refers to.
difficulties.response: Contrast meanings explicitly with the learners' previous systems, treating both as valid in context.

difficulties.pattern: Reluctance to ask about unfamiliar administrative terms.
difficulties.revealedBy: Missed procedures (e.g. extenuating circumstances deadlines) discovered too late.
difficulties.response: Normalise asking and show where answers can be found.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what they would do if they were ill the week an assignment was due, using their institution's terms.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names the correct procedure (extension or extenuating/mitigating circumstances), whom to contact and the evidence needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows to contact someone but uses vague or incorrect terms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know the procedure exists.

guidance.contextNotes: Central at foundation and on pre-sessional courses preparing for progression. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, revisit at key points (first assessments, extenuating circumstances deadlines, dissertation regulations).
reviewNotes: Listed sources support the socialisation and explicitness framing, but no listed study examines institutional vocabulary directly.

guidance.summary: Command words index cognitive processes comparable to those in Anderson and Krathwohl's revised taxonomy, and Horowitz's analysis of actual university assignments showed the range of tasks students must interpret. Moore and Morton found university writing tasks more often require evaluation of others' ideas than test-style opinion essays, so learners from test-focused preparation may misread commands. Teach command words as indicators, not guarantees, and always alongside criteria and exemplars, because tutors use them inconsistently.

activities.title: Command word continuum
learnerActions: Order command words (describe, outline, explain, analyse, compare, evaluate, critically assess) by cognitive demand
For each, note what the answer would contain
Compare your order with marking criteria from your course
activities.intendedInsight: Command words signal different kinds of thinking and text.
activities.rationale: The revised taxonomy offers a shared vocabulary for cognitive processes that command words point to.

activities.title: Same topic, different command
learnerActions: Take one topic and three questions with different commands
Plan an answer to each
Compare plans and identify what changes in structure and content
activities.intendedInsight: The command, not just the topic, determines the answer.
activities.rationale: Horowitz's survey of authentic assignments shows that tasks vary in what they ask students to do, not only in topic.

difficulties.pattern: 'Discuss' means 'give my opinion' or 'write everything I know'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion essays or descriptive overviews in response to 'discuss' questions.
difficulties.response: Show exemplars and criteria that reward balanced, evidence-based discussion leading to a judgement, and make the description–analysis–evaluation distinction explicit.

difficulties.pattern: Commands interpreted from a generic definition list without reading the criteria.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that match a glossary definition but miss what this tutor expects.
difficulties.response: Teach learners to read command, criteria and exemplars together and to ask when unclear.

difficulties.pattern: Secondary commands in multi-part questions overlooked.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers addressing only the first part of 'Explain X and evaluate its effectiveness'.
difficulties.response: Teach systematic question annotation (underline each command and its object).

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What is the difference between “describe” and “evaluate”? Give an example question for each.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that describing reports features while evaluating judges value or effectiveness against criteria, with suitable examples.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Distinguishes them vaguely.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats them as equivalent.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, teach command words explicitly with institutional exemplars. In UG and PGT in-sessional settings, use real module questions and criteria, and discuss variation between tutors.
reviewNotes: Meanings of command words are not standardised across institutions or disciplines; any list of 'definitions' should be presented as typical expectations.
Overlaps with wpr.task-analysis and exm.question-analysis, which could take this topic as a prerequisite.

guidance.summary: Style guides differ on abbreviations: APA, for instance, restricts Latin abbreviations such as 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' to parenthetical material and sets rules for 'et al.', while Chicago has its own conventions. Teach the meaning distinctions (especially e.g. versus i.e.) and then direct learners to their required guide for form and punctuation. The acronym routine — define at first mention, then use consistently — transfers across genres.

activities.title: e.g. or i.e.?
learnerActions: Sort sentences by whether the bracketed material gives examples or restates
Insert 'e.g.' or 'i.e.' accordingly
Check punctuation against your required style guide
activities.intendedInsight: 'e.g.' introduces examples; 'i.e.' restates or specifies.
activities.rationale: Style guides give explicit rules for these abbreviations that learners can apply consistently.

activities.title: Acronym audit
learnerActions: Highlight every acronym in your draft
Check that each is written out in full at first mention
Remove acronyms used only once or twice
activities.intendedInsight: Acronyms help readers only when introduced and used consistently.
activities.rationale: Major style guides require acronyms to be defined at first use.

difficulties.pattern: 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' confused.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'i.e.' followed by one example among many.
difficulties.response: Teach the expansions (for example; that is) and practise.

difficulties.pattern: Acronyms familiar to the writer are left undefined.
difficulties.revealedBy: Undefined field or institutional acronyms in assignments.
difficulties.response: Teach the reader's perspective and the define-at-first-use rule.

difficulties.pattern: Latin abbreviations overused to sound academic.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'viz.', 'cf.' and 'etc.' scattered through running text.
difficulties.response: Show style-guide restrictions and plain English alternatives.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to complete 'Several factors (___ cost and access) affect uptake' and 'The main factor (___ cost) was…' and explain.
diagnostic.strongResponse: 'e.g.' for the first and 'i.e.' for the second, with a correct explanation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One correct.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Both wrong or cannot explain.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional stages, teach core forms with the referencing style in use. In UG in-sessional settings, align with departmental style requirements.
reviewNotes: Conventions are style-guide and edition specific; teachers should check the edition in use.

authorNotes: phr.bundles-text-oriented overlaps with coh.linking-adverbials and coh.connector-precision. I made phr.bundles-text-oriented depend on coh.linking-adverbials; COH authors should not make coh.linking-adverbials depend on PHR topics.

A soft link to sta.metadiscourse was removed because, in the current STA draft, sta.metadiscourse sits after sta.hedging, which already depends on grm.anticipatory-it. STA authors may make sta.hedging or sta.boosters depend on phr.bundles-stance without creating a cycle.

phr.bundles-research-oriented <- phr.collocation-awareness is formally implied by a cross-group chain (grm.np-postmodification -> grm.prepositions -> phr.collocation-awareness). I kept it as distinct and important: awareness of multi-word units is the core dependency, and the grammar route is incidental.

phr.spoken-academic-formulas overlaps with lis.lecture-discourse-markers, lis.relevance-markers, coh.spoken-signposting and prs.signposting. Those topics could take it as a prerequisite; I have not linked in the other direction.
The skeleton has no participant-oriented bundle topic as such (Hyland's third category); it is partly covered by phr.bundles-stance. This seems acceptable.
phr.verb-noun-collocation-accuracy is mainly a remediation topic; it could arguably be merged into phr.academic-collocations, but keeping it separate allows a distinct diagnostic and error-log focus.

reg.impersonality-presence overlaps with sta.self-mention. Suggested division: REG covers the impersonal/personal choice and its rhetorical consequences; STA covers the pronoun system and authorial roles. If STA links them, sta.self-mention should depend on reg.impersonality-presence (or neither should link), not the reverse, to avoid a cycle with reg.disciplinary-style.

reg.vague-overgeneralised overlaps with sta.generalisation-qualification. I have placed the REG topic earlier (B1–B2+, foundation onwards) with no STA prerequisite; sta.generalisation-qualification could take it as a prerequisite.

reg.information-density overlaps with sen.concision, sen.clarity-end-weight and grm.nominalisation. If SEN authors link these, the natural direction is sen.clarity-end-weight -> reg.information-density or no link; reg.information-density depends on grm.nominalisation and grm.phrasal-complexity.

reg.non-specialist-audiences overlaps with pub.research-engagement and grp.public-writing (genres) and res.ethics-documentation (participant information). Those topics should take reg.non-specialist-audiences as a prerequisite.

The skeleton has no topic on register in digital/informal academic channels (forum posts, messaging) beyond prg.messaging-channels; reg.register-awareness covers the concept but a short note in PRG would help.

voc.abstract-shell-nouns overlaps substantially with coh.signalling-nouns and grm.reference-pronouns ('this + summarising noun'). Suggested division: VOC owns the lexical set and its patterns; COH owns cohesive deployment; GRM owns pronoun/demonstrative reference. COH and GRM topics can take voc.abstract-shell-nouns as a prerequisite; I have not linked in the reverse direction.
voc.academic-verbs overlaps with src.reporting-verbs and sta.boosters/sta.hedging (verb strength). Suggested: src.reporting-verbs depends on voc.academic-verbs.
voc.evaluative-lexis overlaps with sta.attitude-markers and sta.evaluating-others-language; those should depend on it rather than the reverse.
voc.technical-terminology overlaps with coh.terminological-consistency and fun.defining; I deliberately did not make it depend on fun.defining so that fun.defining can depend on it.

To avoid a cycle I removed my edge. Either direction is defensible; an integrator should choose one deliberately.
